name: Amira Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Amira, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign for anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. This is a made-up study built around people like you, and there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays are lectures in digital logic, calculus and a C programming course, then a lab on Wednesday where we solder a small amplifier. I eat lunch with the same three people every day, and I go to bed before eleven because I don't function otherwise. On Fridays I take the train home to my parents' town, and on Sunday morning I sing in the church choir, then eat with my grandparents. It's the part of the week I miss most when I'm away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What led you to computer engineering?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My grandfather started a furniture workshop, and my father runs it now with six workers. I grew up watching how a machine and a craftsman fit together. I was the top of my class, and my parents pay my fees and my room, so I have no debt. I like understanding how things are built from the inside, and I don't use AI tools, because I want to know my work is mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it's what sensible people said all along. Not everything new is better, and not everything old is stupid. I'd tell my friends we can use a tool when it helps and put it down when it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel relieved but not completely easy. My father's workshop has had a hard few years with cheap imports and rising wood prices, and that isn't AI. I'd still be thinking about whether the family business survives until I graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, work hard on my labs, and spend the summer in my father's workshop, helping with the ordering and the books. I'd keep singing in the choir and keep my weekends for family. I'd also ask the university about an apprenticeship-style placement, because I believe you learn best by doing the work next to someone experienced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady. Quiet, like a village after the harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the workshop has had hard years. How worried are you about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried enough that I'd stay home for a month if my father asked me to. The workshop is how my family earned its living for sixty years. I don't want to be the one who watches my family's workshop go because I was busy with my own plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to happen to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my father to be able to keep going until he's ready to stop, with good workers who know their trade. If I could add a small online shop to sell the chairs, I'd do that, even though I don't love putting things online.

say: I'd say not everything new is better, and not everything old is **stupid**.
I'd tell friends to use a tool when it helps and **put it down** when it doesn't.
think: I'd feel relieved but not **easy**, because my father's workshop already struggles with imports and wood prices.
I wonder if the **family business** survives until I graduate.
do: Work in my father's **workshop** over the summer, helping with ordering and books.
Ask the university about a **placement** next to an experienced engineer.
Keep singing in the **choir** and keep weekends for family.
feel: Steady and **quiet**, like a village after the harvest.
S0.quote: I don't want to be the one who watches my family's workshop go because I was busy with my own plans.
fieldNote: Her unease in a quiet world comes from the **family workshop**, which already struggles with imports and prices.
Prefers learning by doing next to someone experienced, in line with her traditional values.
Dislikes putting things online, yet would open a small online shop if needed.

steps.text: Spend the summer helping with ordering and books at the workshop
Ask the university about a hands-on engineering placement
Keep studying and keep weekends for family and choir

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be careful about handing thinking to machines, and that the sensible response is work and skill, not complaining. I'd tell my friends to learn a real trade or craft next to their degree, because hands-on skill will hold its value longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel concerned. Coding is one of the things the card says AI takes first, and I'm studying a degree with a lot of coding. I don't use the tools, so I feel I'm doing things the slow way. But my father's work is hands-on, and that lasts, so I'd feel I have something to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying but lean toward hardware, electronics and control systems. I'd do a placement at a factory or an engineering firm, not a software house. I'd learn to use one AI tool in a limited way, because I can't refuse everything, and I'd ask my father to teach me the workshop machinery on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a heavy cloud, not a storm. I still go to choir and the cloud follows me there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible for this change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The large technology companies, mostly. They push these tools on everyone, and then ask governments for rules that protect themselves. I'd also blame governments that gave them cheap money and hoped for the best. Ordinary people didn't ask for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of help would you accept, and not accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd accept training and apprenticeships, even paid ones. I'd not like being handed money for doing nothing, because people want work that matters. But if my father's workshop had a bad year I'd accept help with taxes or a fair loan.

I'd tell friends to learn a real **craft** next to their degree.
think: I feel **concerned**, since coding is one of the first things the card says AI takes.
My father's hands-on work gives me something to fall back on, which I'd value **more**.
do: Lean toward **hardware**, electronics and control systems.
Do a placement at a **factory** or engineering firm, not a software house.

feel: Like a heavy **cloud**, not a storm, that follows me to choir.
S1.quote: I'd accept training and apprenticeships, even paid ones. I'd not like being handed money for doing nothing, because people want work that matters.
fieldNote: Her **values** shape the response: apprenticeships over handouts, work that matters.
Blames tech companies and governments that gave them cheap money, not ordinary people.
Moves toward hands-on engineering and the family trade as a hedge.

steps.text: Choose hardware, electronics and control systems modules
Apply for a placement at a factory or engineering firm

Try one AI tool in a limited, supervised way

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this can't be allowed to happen without a plan. People need work, and families need time. I'd say governments should slow the companies down and support apprenticeships and families first, and I'd say it loudly, even if my friends call it old-fashioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be terrified. In two years, the kind of work I'm training for could be done by software, and I wouldn't have even finished my first year. My father's workshop would last longer because wood and hands take robots until around 2031, but the ordering, the design, and the customers would all change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home on weekends and spend more time in the workshop. I'd ask my father if I could learn the craft side properly, even if I stay at university. I'd save every bit of money I can, and cut anything I don't need. I'd rely on my church community and family, because those are the people who'd help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a stone in my chest. I'd keep going to choir because singing helps, but I'd be crying in the car park.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the degree is still worth finishing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes, because quitting in a panic is worse. A degree teaches you how a machine thinks, and that helps even if the job isn't the one I imagined. But I'd also not put all my hope in it. I'd have a second plan, in the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should stay together, spend carefully, and not borrow for anything. I'd say I'll learn the workshop trade properly. My mother would cry, and my father would say we've survived worse, which is his way of saying he's scared too.

I'd urge governments to slow the companies and back **apprenticeships**.
think: I'd be **terrified**: the work I'm training for could be done by software.
The workshop lasts longer, but ordering, design and **customers** change at once.

S2.quote: Quitting in a panic is worse. A degree teaches you how a machine thinks, and that helps even if the job isn't the one I imagined.
fieldNote: Frightened but **practical**: stays at university and builds a second plan in the workshop.
Leans on church, family and her father's resilience rather than on the state.
Anxious rather than alarmed because the family has a workshop and savings to fall back on.

steps.text: Learn the workshop's craft side every weekend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and sensible people use it. I'd say my generation should learn real skills, and that communities should look after each other while this happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious but more hopeful than in the first one. I'd graduate in three years, which is awkward timing, but I'd have time to build skills that last, like electronics and some craft. The robots come around 2034, so my father's trade has a bit more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree with a focus on hardware and control. I'd do two summers in the workshop and one in a factory. I'd start saving steadily, and I'd ask my father to hand me some of the workshop's ordering and accounts so I understand the business. I'd probably begin using a simple AI tool for the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long winter you can see coming. You stack firewood, you check the roof, and you wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from the two-year picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be shaking. With five, I'd be preparing. I'd feel responsible for the workshop, but I'd have time to learn to run it, not just save it in an emergency. That's a very different feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, for dull jobs in the workshop's accounts, once someone I trust has used them for a while. I'd not use it for my coursework. That feels like giving away something I'm supposed to be building in myself.

I'd say communities should **look after** each other.
think: I'd feel **anxious** but more hopeful, with time for skills that last.
The robots come around 2034, so my father's trade has more **time**.

Spend two summers in the **workshop** and one in a factory.

S3.quote: With two years, I'd be shaking. With five, I'd be preparing.
fieldNote: Time converts her fear into **preparation** for running the workshop, her own phrase.

steps.text: Take hardware and control modules for the final two years
Spend two summers in the workshop and one in a factory
Take over the workshop's ordering and accounts
Use a simple AI tool for workshop paperwork, not coursework

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to prepare if people stay patient and don't panic. I'd say families should plan together, and schools should teach work and trades as well as theory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel mostly at ease, but still watchful. Ten years takes me through the degree and a first job, and by then I'd have real experience. My father might retire by then, and I'd have a choice about whether the workshop continues with me or with someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and finish my degree, work a few years in industry, and keep my ties to the workshop. I'd save for a deposit on a home near my parents. I'd not rush to use new tools, but I'd learn the ones that matter once the people I trust have used them for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels peaceful. Like Sunday after church, when the week's problems seem smaller for a few hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have in place by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family that's secure, a workshop that's either thriving or sold at a fair price, and enough skill that I can work anywhere. I'd also want my grandparents to be looked after. They'd be very old, and that's where I think my own duty would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about your approach if the date moved closer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move faster on learning the workshop and on talking to my family about money. I might even leave the degree if it clearly wasn't leading anywhere, which would be painful. But I'd decide with my parents, not alone.

I'd say schools should teach **trades** as well as theory.
think: I'd feel mostly **at ease** but watchful.
By then my father might retire, so the **workshop** question would be mine.

feel: **Peaceful**, like Sunday after church when the week's problems seem smaller.
S4.quote: I'd decide with my parents, not alone.
fieldNote: Duty to **family** shapes her plans: grandparents' care, the workshop, a home nearby.
Would adjust fast if the date moved, even considering leaving the degree, but only with her parents.

steps.text: Finish the degree and work a few years in industry

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits my family's workshop and my own plans together, and nobody has time to prepare. What would help is apprenticeships and training that pay a fair wage, and some support for family businesses while they change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people who prefer old ways aren't foolish. I don't use the tools, and I'm not afraid of the future. I'd just like the future to move at a pace families can keep up with.

headlineQuote: I'd just like the future to move at a pace families can keep up with.
portrait: Amira is an 18-year-old **computer engineering** student from a furniture-workshop family, who doesn't use AI tools.
She is traditional in outlook: choir, grandparents, apprenticeships over handouts, and decisions made with her parents.
Her main worry is the **family workshop**, which already struggles, and her own degree timing.
Her hedge is hands-on craft; she moves toward hardware and learns the workshop on weekends.
She moves from uneasy to **anxious** as the warning time falls, and eases back with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, since it hits the workshop and her plans together with no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** and paid training, plus support for family businesses while they change.
